title: Hubble looks at sideways NGC 4710 (full)
caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4710, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4710 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4710, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on. Look straight at its centre and you can make out a faint, ghostly X-shaped structure.

Astronomers call a feature like this a boxy or peanut-shaped bulge. It comes from stars in the galaxy's bar moving up and down, out of the plane of the disc, and it is only visible when a galaxy is viewed edge-on. From other angles, the structure is not evident.

How the central bulges of spiral galaxies form and change is still an open question, and that puzzle is what drew astronomers to NGC 4710. The galaxy is also a bit of an oddity. Peanut-shaped bulges are often seen in spirals with small bulges and loosely wound arms, but they are less common in galaxies like NGC 4710, whose arms wrap tightly around a more prominent bulge.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.27 x 1.68 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 57,000 × 29,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The faint X-shape is subtle even in Hubble's image, and the galaxy is far too dim to see in this detail by eye; part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect.

explore: NGC 4710 lies about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. The edge-on view hides its spiral arms but lets astronomers see the vertical shape of its centre.
alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a faint X-shaped structure visible at its centre.
